summaries.headline: Tennessee Republicans Block Districts From Fighting State Takeovers
summaries.summary: Tennessee Republicans passed legislation preventing school districts from using their budgets to fund lawsuits challenging state accountability measures, including potential takeovers, though districts could still pursue legal action if outside organizations pay the bills. The bill, sponsored by Sen. Brent Taylor and backed by takeover proponents, comes as lawmakers prepare to unveil renewed efforts to seize control from Memphis-Shelby County's elected school board. The timing mirrors Houston's strategy, where the local district delayed a state takeover for three years through costly litigation before ultimately losing at the Texas Supreme Court.

summaries.headline: Utah District Seeks K-5 Computer Science Platform
summaries.summary: Granite School District in Utah is soliciting computer science courses for its 60,000 students in grades K-5, seeking a platform with pre-created coding courses aligned to state standards. The district wants comprehensive, developmentally appropriate content that integrates with its existing physical computing devices including VEX Go, VEX 123, and Code & Go Mice, plus robust analytics and training support. The April 15 deadline reflects growing pressure on elementary schools to build foundational computer science skills as state requirements expand beyond traditional high school offerings.

summaries.headline: Florida School Builds AI Into Every Classroom Experience
summaries.summary: The Jewish Leadership Academy in Florida designed its classrooms from opening in 2023 to automatically record lessons using AI-powered tools that catalog and time-stamp content for student review. Students can search recorded classes for specific spoken words or screen text through their learning management system, while teachers use AI to generate lesson plans and lecture summaries. The school's "hyper learning" model demonstrates how purpose-built infrastructure can make personalized, on-demand instruction a seamless part of daily operations rather than an add-on technology.

summaries.headline: Arizona Program Coaches Parents as First Reading Teachers
summaries.summary: Story School, a partnership between Read On Chandler and Make Way for Books, targets families without preschool access by teaching parents to build early literacy skills in children from birth to age 5. The 12-session program fills a critical intervention gap during the years when language and literacy develop fastest, addressing Arizona's broader challenge where children who aren't reading at grade level by third grade are significantly less likely to graduate high school on time. The approach recognizes that closing reading gaps requires reaching families before formal schooling begins, particularly in communities where traditional early childhood programs remain out of reach.

summaries.headline: Wisconsin School Uses AI to Streamline Behavior Interventions
summaries.summary: Holmen Middle School in Wisconsin is using Google's Gemini AI to help its behavior intervention team develop student support plans aligned with the district's social-emotional learning playbook. The 900-student school's administrative team and single behavior interventionist use the custom AI assistant to brainstorm intervention ideas without inputting personally identifiable student information, focusing instead on generic situational details. Associate Principal Ben Tashner reports the AI provides simplified suggestions that often surface approaches the team hadn't considered, adding another layer to their collaborative decision-making process for supporting students with behavioral challenges.

summaries.headline: NYC Schools Cut $58 Million, Bigger Reductions Coming
summaries.summary: New York City's Education Department trimmed $58.8 million from its budget as Mayor Zohran Mamdani pushes to close a multi-billion dollar budget gap, but officials acknowledge this represents only a fraction of required cuts. The reductions target central office spending on supplies, professional development, and travel this year, with contract terminations and spending caps planned for next year. The department faces pressure to find over $800 million in total savings across two fiscal years, yet city officials have declined to release the full savings plan or confirm exact targets.

summaries.headline: NYC Deploys 18-Year-Olds as School Safety Officers
summaries.summary: New York City has stationed 114 assistant school safety agents as young as 18 in elementary schools to address a staffing crisis that has reduced police presence in schools by 28% over six years. The assistant agents, earning $37,339 annually, handle front desk duties, operate video intercoms, and help identify rule violations while regular school safety agent ranks have dropped from 5,000 to fewer than 3,600 since 2020. School leaders worry the overall decline in safety staffing has compromised security and created operational delays, pushing the district to fill gaps with recent high school graduates in quasi-police roles.

summaries.headline: NYC Releases AI Guidelines, Leaves Key Questions Unresolved
summaries.summary: New York City's Education Department released preliminary AI guidelines using a traffic light system that allows teacher lesson planning tools while prohibiting AI from making decisions about student grading, discipline, or special education placements. The guidance leaves major questions unanswered, including whether students can use AI for homework or access personal chatbot accounts beyond district-approved tools, with public feedback being collected through May 8 before a final version in June. The framework arrives nearly three years after the district's brief ChatGPT ban, as many schools had already developed their own AI policies while waiting for citywide direction.

summaries.headline: NYC Schools Create AI Policies While District Delays
summaries.summary: New York City schools have developed their own artificial intelligence policies after more than two years of waiting for district-wide guidance, with approaches ranging from comprehensive 12-page documents to complete classroom bans. East Side Community School's assistant principal spent months crafting detailed rules around "unsupervised use of generative AI" after staff found themselves holding multiple weekly meetings with students suspected of inappropriate AI use. The patchwork of school-level responses highlights the complex challenge facing the Education Department as it prepares to release its long-awaited citywide policy on Tuesday, with educators and parents split between those calling for complete moratoriums and those arguing students need exposure to transformative workplace technology.

summaries.headline: NYC Prepares for Life After Regents Exams
summaries.summary: New York City educators face their final year of Regents exam requirements before the state transitions to its Portrait of a Graduate framework in 2027-28, which evaluates students on six qualities including critical thinking and global citizenship rather than standardized test scores. Chancellor Kamar Samuels has restructured his leadership team to include a new high school position headed by Alan Cheng, signaling the district's intent to "ramp up" implementation planning, though state officials have provided limited specifics on how students will demonstrate mastery of the new criteria. The shift from test-based to competency-based graduation requirements represents one of the most significant changes to New York's accountability system in decades, leaving educators to navigate the transition with broad guidelines around research projects and internships but few concrete assessment details.

summaries.headline: Wisconsin Democrats Propose $1.3B Education Boost From Surplus
summaries.summary: Democratic State Reps. Angelina Cruz and Christian Phelps want to use $1.3 billion of Wisconsin's $2.5 billion budget surplus to increase general school aid and raise special education reimbursement rates to 60%. The proposal would add nearly $446 million to general school aid for 2026-27, aimed at reducing property tax burdens that have risen up to 29% in some districts like Kenosha. With regular legislative sessions concluded for the term, the plan highlights the ongoing tension between state funding formulas and local districts' growing reliance on referendums to maintain operations.

summaries.headline: Arizona Governor Halts Budget Talks Over School Funding
summaries.summary: Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs suspended budget negotiations with Republican lawmakers over disagreements on public school funding levels. The breakdown comes as districts across the state face ongoing financial pressures and lawmakers debate competing priorities for education investments. The stalled talks signal another year of uncertainty for Arizona school leaders trying to plan staffing and programs without knowing their final budget allocations.

summaries.headline: Michigan District Bans All Screens Mid-Year
summaries.summary: Mesick Consolidated Schools eliminated Chromebooks and tablets from its 250-student elementary school last month after a conversation revealed that teachers had largely stopped reading aloud to students. The rural district's third-grade reading proficiency sits at just 18% — half the state average and half what it was a decade ago — prompting leaders to view screens as barriers to literacy development. The overnight ban reflects growing nationwide skepticism about classroom technology's impact on learning, as districts search for solutions to persistent achievement declines.

summaries.headline: Two Candidates Seek IPS Board Seat Amid Crisis
summaries.summary: The Indianapolis Public Schools board will select between two applicants to fill the vacant District 2 seat left by Gayle Cosby's resignation due to health challenges. Assistant professor Bryan Duarte, who has questioned the new state education oversight corporation, faces community advocate Hasaan Rashid, who previously ran for the seat with backing from school choice groups. The appointment comes as IPS projects a $40 million cash deficit and awaits voter approval of a crucial property tax increase in November.

summaries.headline: Research Identifies Four Strategies to Improve Student Focus
summaries.summary: One-quarter of public schools report that student inattention severely impacts learning, with elementary engagement typically dropping after 10 minutes of activity. Research confirms that smartphones tax mental resources during classwork, but educators can strengthen on-task behavior through strategic classroom design and teaching practices. Studies show that implementation intentions—teaching students automatic "when X happens, I do Y" responses—along with clear task instructions, purposeful movement breaks, and consistent routines help create conditions that support sustained attention during complex academic work.

summaries.headline: Albany County Pilots AI Platform to Combat Absenteeism
summaries.summary: Albany County launched an AI-powered pilot program with Ravena-Coeymans-Selkirk Central School District to address chronic absenteeism affecting 26 percent of students across the county's 12 districts — more than 9,000 of 35,000 total students. The Edia platform automatically texts families in their preferred language when absences occur, captures reasons and documentation, and analyzes patterns to identify root causes like transportation issues or family crises, with the company claiming a 30 percent reduction in chronic absenteeism. The county investment reflects growing recognition that attendance technology may offer scalable solutions for a persistent post-pandemic challenge that affects more than one in four students nationwide.

summaries.headline: Pennsylvania Senate Advances Four School Policy Bills
summaries.summary: Pennsylvania's Senate Education Committee approved four bills addressing curriculum transparency, student data privacy, emergency medical care, and POW/MIA recognition requirements for schools. The measures include mandating online posting of course curriculum information, establishing student data privacy protections, allowing voluntary administration of anti-seizure medication to students with epilepsy, and requiring POW/MIA flag displays at public schools. The legislative package reflects ongoing state-level efforts to balance parental access to school information with student safety protections, while addressing both health emergencies and civic education requirements.

summaries.headline: Andhra Pradesh Hires School Counselors for Mental Health
summaries.summary: Andhra Pradesh became the first Indian state to appoint dedicated mental health counselors at the school level, placing at least one counselor in every mandal to address rising student mental health concerns. State officials emphasized the counselors' role in preventing substance abuse and student suicides, with plans to conduct psychometric assessments for eighth and ninth graders in June to evaluate intellectual abilities. The initiative reflects growing recognition that early intervention systems require dedicated staffing rather than adding responsibilities to existing educators.

summaries.headline: Boston Teachers Rally Against Hundreds of Job Cuts
summaries.summary: Boston teachers and parents rallied outside City Hall Tuesday as the district's proposed budget threatens to eliminate hundreds of positions, including 105 special education paraprofessionals and 142 multilingual education staff. The Boston Teachers Union argues these cuts would disproportionately impact a workforce that is more than 70 percent Black and Latino, while advocates push for an additional $48 million in city funding to maintain current staffing levels. The timing puts pressure on city leaders who are celebrating the district's highest graduation rate in history while deciding whether to sustain the support systems that helped achieve those gains.

summaries.headline: Intuit Offers Hour-Long Financial Literacy Classroom Activities
summaries.summary: Intuit has launched a free financial literacy challenge that allows educators to introduce money management concepts in a single class period with minimal preparation time. The Hour of Finance Challenge runs through April 15, 2026, and provides interactive games focused on credit and budgeting decisions that require only laptops or tablets, with participating schools eligible for supplies funding. The plug-and-play format addresses a persistent challenge for educators who want to incorporate financial education but lack time for extensive lesson planning or subject-matter expertise.

This spring, plant something.

How many people does it take to plant a tree?

One. You already know the answer. You could do it this weekend, alone, with a shovel and a sapling, and that tree would grow.

But here is the question we should actually be asking: How many people does it take to grow a forest? To shade every school playground in Minnesota? To restore hundreds of acres of prairie and clean the water running through it? That number is bigger. And it turns out, we have it.

Minnesota stands to lose an estimated $41 million in federal clean water funding under proposed Environmental Protection Agency cuts, cuts that the Minnesota Department of Health says would “greatly impair” our ability to keep water safe. The federal government is not coming to save our prairies, our waterways or our neighborhoods. That work is falling to us.

Minnesotans already know how to do this. Thirty years ago, thousands of people showed up along the Mississippi River in St. Paul with shovels and trees and got to work. They restored a riverfront that had been degraded for decades, replanted trees along a critical migratory flyway and built something the whole city now takes pride in. Nobody waited for a perfect political moment or federal dollars. They just planted. That effort became Great River Greening, and in the years since, we have restored more than 60,000 acres across Minnesota — prairies, wetlands, forests, shorelines — one site, one volunteer, one seed at a time.

I invite you to join us this spring and do something that will matter both today and decades from now. Help restore tree canopy in Bemidji after last summer’s devastating storms. Plant native violets at Lamberton Wildlife Management Area to support the rare regal fritillary butterfly, which depends on them to survive. Remove invasive species at Big Stone National Wildlife Refuge at the headwaters of the Minnesota River. Or plant trees along the Mississippi River at Lilydale Regional Park, where this all started 30 years ago.

How many people does it take to plant a forest? To grow a canopy, clean a river, restore a prairie, and ensure that Minnesota looks like Minnesota in 50 years? It turns out the answer is the same as it was 30 years ago on the banks of the Mississippi. It takes all of us, one person at a time, planting one tree, one wildflower, one seed. We can do that. We can do it this spring. And unlike a lot of what feels out of reach right now, this is something we can do with our own two hands. Not one of us. All of us.

_Kateri Routh, St. Paul_

_The writer is executive director of Great River Greening._

##### EDUCATION

## Walz’s budget cuts what needs saving

Minnesotans deserve a budget that reflects our priorities and meets the real needs of students and families. Unfortunately, the supplemental budget proposal recently put forward by Gov. Tim Walz falls short in some key areas that deserve serious attention.

First, the proposal includes an additional $50 million cut to special education, bringing the total reduction to $300 million. Schools across our state are already working to manage growing costs and increasing demands, especially when it comes to serving students with special needs. Reducing support in this area only puts more pressure on school districts, educators and, ultimately, the students who rely on these services the most. If we are serious about supporting every student, we should be strengthening special education funding, not scaling it back.

The proposal also takes aim at an effort I have been working on to bring more educational opportunity into Minnesota. Specifically, it suggests that if our state opts into the federal Scholarship Granting Organization (SGO) tax credit program, there would be cuts to nonpublic pupil aid and transportation funding. That approach misses the mark.

The reality is that Minnesotans are already eligible to donate to SGOs in other states and receive a federal tax credit for doing so. Right now, those dollars can’t be directed to help students here in Minnesota because we have not opted into the program. That means money is leaving our state instead of supporting local families and schools. Opting in would simply allow those same contributions to stay here at home, expanding opportunities without raising taxes or taking resources away from public schools. Securing funding for schools in unique ways such as this, which do so without raising taxes, is absolutely critical at this time.

Framing this as a tradeoff that requires cuts to other areas is misleading and unnecessary. We should be looking for ways to bring additional resources into Minnesota and give families more options, not setting up false choices that limit opportunity.

At the end of the day, this comes down to priorities. We need to focus on policies that strengthen our education system across the board, support students with the greatest needs, and make smart and strategic use of available resources. That includes ensuring accountability in how taxpayer dollars are spent and making sure funding decisions reflect what’s actually happening in our schools and communities.

I will continue to advocate for a more balanced and practical approach as the legislative process moves forward. Minnesota students, families and schools deserve thoughtful solutions that expand opportunity and provide real support where it’s needed most. Moreover, I will certainly not vote for any additional cuts proposed by Walz.

_Ron Kresha, Little Falls, Minn._

##### ACTIVISM

## Who’s against engaged students?

In response to Katherine Kersten’s opinion piece “ [For years, Walz has been priming students to become activists](https://www.startribune.com/mn-k12-education-ethnic-studies-race-theory/601597702 "https://www.startribune.com/mn-k12-education-ethnic-studies-race-theory/601597702")” (Strib Voices, March 16): I find it hard to imagine why becoming an “activist” isn’t what we all should aspire to be. Do we not want all our citizens to participate actively in our government? Isn’t she an activist in participating in the political arena as she does? She did not define what an activist actually is, but I can only imagine in her opinion it is someone who is opposed to her ideas. Where was she during the ‘60s and ‘70s when we were protesting an unjust war and were successful in exposing the truth of the war?

I can only hope that all of us continue to be activists and are proud of it.

_Elisa Wright, Bloomington_

# As Triton budget balloons, local officials beg legislators to overhaul school funding formula

ROWLEY — The Triton Regional School District has reached a breaking point.

Despite rising education costs, the district has been receiving minimal state aid for years due to shrinking enrollment, leaving taxpayers to shoulder the burden.

Local officials are now saying their towns just can’t do it anymore. There is nothing left to cut in their town budgets, they say, leaving voters to decide between funding the school or essential services.

At a meeting earlier this month, local officials begged legislators to overhaul the state’s school-funding formula, warning that Triton and its communities are headed for financial ruin.

“I don’t know how our towns and our district are going to survive another five years,” said Nerissa Wallen, Rowley’s representative on the Triton School Committee.

“I don’t know where we go from here, and I don’t know how we ask for more help than we’re already asking for,” she added.

## A broken funding formula

Since 2002, Triton’s operating expenses have increased by $28 million, but Chapter 70 aid has only increased $773,000, according to Newbury Select Chair Bill DiMaio.

Chapter 70 is the state’s primary education funding formula. It is partially based on enrollment, which has become a problem for Triton and scores of districts across the state where enrollment is declining.

Despite the shrinking numbers, the state has ensured that schools won’t receive less aid than the year before through a provision in the formula called “hold harmless.”

Under the provision, districts that have lower enrollment still get the same aid as the year before. They also get a certain amount of money per pupil — this year, that amount was $150.

While Sen. Bruce Tarr has pushed for increases in aid, he said it’s a “short-term strategy at best.” Roughly 270 of 318 districts in the state only receive minimum per pupil aid, he noted — evidence that the formula isn’t working.

Another issue with the Chapter 70 formula is that it overestimates communities’ ability to pay for education while underestimating education costs, Tarr said.

The formula determines the minimum spending requirements for each town in a district, partially by assessing home value. It sees the relatively high value of homes on the North Shore and fails to account for the income of the residents, according to Tarr.

It also underestimates the costs of special education, insurance, and inflation, he said.

“The values of what you can pay are overinflated, the assumptions of what education costs are under assumed … so the delta of what Chapter 70 is just keeps shrinking,” Triton Superintendent Brian Forget said.

## Strain on towns

As state aid has declined, the financial responsibility placed on Triton’s communities has increased significantly.

Rowley, Newbury, and Salisbury are now responsible for funding 80% of Triton’s $57.2 million budget, Alicia Greco, vice chair of the Newbury Select Board, noted. In 2002, the three communities were responsible for less than 60% of the budget, according to Forget.

In order to fund the school budget, the towns have been relying on residential property taxes. None of them have large enough commercial bases to [shift the tax rate](https://thelocalnews.news/2025/12/08/rowley-maintains-flat-tax-rate-for-fy26/) onto, officials said.

But the towns can only raise their property taxes so much — Proposition 2 ½, a Massachusetts law, limits property tax increases to 2.5% a year. The Triton budget, however, has historically increased between 4% and 6% a year.

This leaves town voters in a difficult position where they must decide whether to fund the increasing school budget or town services. Voters can also allow the town to raise taxes higher than 2.5% through an override, but that quickly becomes unsustainable for many households.

“The people that … cannot afford it — it’s not just the elderly,” Rowley Select Chair Sheri David said. “It’s across the board, people are struggling, and we just don’t know what to tell them.”

## Sea change

Many local officials were especially frustrated to hear that the state has seen a boom in its budget. The Millionaires Tax was projected to generate between $1 billion and $2 billion, Tarr said, but the number is now somewhere between $3 billion and $4 billion.

“When I hear a number like $3 or $4 billion that ‘might’ make its way back here, I’m disgusted,” Newbury Finance Committee Chair Erica Jacobsen said. “We’re all fighting over property tax increases at the local level.”

When Jacobsen accused the legislators of not bringing significant funding to Triton in the past 15 years, Tarr pointed to increases they have secured in special education funding and transportation.

“I feel like we’re at the point where a little bit here or a little bit there, this could’ve helped us five years ago, maybe,” Wallen said. “We’re at the point right now that, unless there is a sea change, we will not be here.”

That “sea change” has to be a total reform of Chapter 70, according to Forget.

“Anything else is an appreciated Band-Aid, but it doesn’t solve any of the problems,” he said.

## Building a coalition

The challenge with reforming Chapter 70 will be getting legislators to agree on how to change it, according to Tarr.

“It’s often said … that if you ask all 200 legislators what to do about Chapter 70, you’ll get 201 opinions,” he said.

The rural and suburban communities need to unite around a particular issue, like how the formula underrecognizes special education costs or health insurance increases, Tarr said, and push for reform in that area.

“It isn’t that some of these things aren’t being raised on the floor — some people thought I was going to have a cardiac arrest this past week in this debate,” Tarr said. “The problem is, how do we get enough people to say this has to happen, and what is it that the ‘this’ is?”

Rep. Kristin Kassner said she has seen more cohesion among districts as the number of schools in “hold harmless” has increased. She has also seen more conversation among rural schools in Western Massachusetts, leading her to hope for unification and change.

## ‘No faith’

Salisbury Selectman Michael Colburn told local officials the three towns need to come together to solve the crisis on their own, saying he has “no faith” the legislators are going to help Triton.

“If you have substance and you can actually help us and not just throw crumbs at the floor and expect us to get on our hands and knees to eat it, I’m willing to listen,” Colburn told legislators. “But until that changes, I really don’t wanna hear it no more.”

Wallen, however, said Triton “cannot close any doors” and asked the legislators to keep working with the district to push for reform.

“We have to overturn every rock to try and keep things here for our towns and for our schools,” she said. “This is a problem. Communities are dying, and this is what it looks like.”

local_articles.full_content:

[Alaska Legislature](https://www.adn.com/politics/alaska-legislature/)

# Alaska House majority seeks to guarantee $158M increase in public school funding

By [Iris Samuels](https://www.adn.com/author/iris-samuels), [Mari Kanagy](https://www.adn.com/author/mari-kanagy)

Published: March 24, 2026

![](https://www.adn.com/resizer/v2/ABQMRJMUPFB7BPUFDNPR5GIS5I.JPG?auth=f24a5cfea9fc2a8134e044fcdc8d609872ae92c76025947f2bae91c603cac310&width=800&height=533)The entrance to the House of Representatives Chamber at the Alaska State Capitol in Juneau on Feb. 26, 2024. (Marc Lester / ADN)

The House Finance Committee introduced a new operating budget draft on Tuesday that, if adopted, would guarantee a $158 million increase in funding for Alaska public schools the next fiscal year.

The state already spends around $1.3 billion to provide a public education to roughly 125,000 K-12 students in Alaska. The Legislature last year approved an update to the base formula used to calculate per-school funding that amounted to a roughly $175 million increase in base spending, after several years in which lawmakers approved one-time funding increases without changing the base formula.

It was the first time the formula increased significantly under Gov. Mike Dunleavy; lawmakers twice [overrode](https://www.adn.com/politics/alaska-legislature/2025/08/02/alaska-legislature-briefly-delays-joint-session-amid-plans-to-vote-on-overriding-governors-vetoes/) Dunleavy’s vetoes to cement the formula change.

But school districts across the state have said that last year’s formula update was insufficient to keep up with rising costs. In effect, state education spending has not kept up with inflation during Dunleavy’s tenure.

Many districts, including those in Anchorage and the Matanuska-Susitna Borough, face multimillion-dollar [deficits](https://www.akleg.gov/basis/get_documents.asp?session=34&docid=11291) and depleted reserves that have caused them to order school closures, increase class sizes and cut programs.

This session,members of the Alaska House are calling again for the formula to be updated. A bill working its way through the chamber would [increase](https://www.adn.com/alaska-news/2026/03/19/alaska-senate-education-bill-raises-debate-over-correspondence-funding/ "https://www.adn.com/alaska-news/2026/03/19/alaska-senate-education-bill-raises-debate-over-correspondence-funding/") the Base Student Allocation from $6,660 to $7,290, translating to a $158 million boost in education funding in the coming fiscal year.

The boost would [translate](https://www.akleg.gov/basis/get_documents.asp?session=34&docid=11295 "https://www.akleg.gov/basis/get_documents.asp?session=34&docid=11295") to $44 million in extra funding for the Anchorage School District; $22 million for the Mat-Su Borough School District; and $14 million for the Fairbanks North Star Borough School District.

ADVERTISEMENT

Budgeters in the Finance Committee on Tuesday indicated that if that bill doesn’t pass, they would seek one-time funding of an equal amount to be included in the coming year’s budget.

Educators in recent years have decried one-time funding, which has increasingly been used amid political opposition to permanent formula changes. Such funding cannot be used for long-term planning, school leaders reason, limiting its utility.

House Finance Co-Chair Andy Josephson, an Anchorage Democrat, said that despite the limitations of one-time funding, Dunleavy “had been relatively amenable” to increasing education spending outside of the permanent formula. On the other hand, Josephson said Dunleavy has been “very unamenable to funding through any BSA growth.”

“Because the BSA is a difficult thing to pass, we think that this backstop is critically important,” Josephson later added.

ADVERTISEMENT

In 2024, Dunleavy allowed $175 million in one-time school funding to remain on the books, even as he opposed increasing the permanent formula by a similar amount.

Dunleavy has a long track record of vetoing one-time school operations and maintenance funding. Last year, he attempted to veto over $50 million for school operations, only to be overridden by lawmakers. He also [vetoed](https://www.adn.com/politics/2025/06/12/gov-dunleavy-vetoes-51m-school-funding-from-budget/) $25 million in school maintenance funding. In 2023, Dunleavy [vetoed](https://www.adn.com/politics/alaska-legislature/2023/06/19/dunleavy-vetoes-more-than-87-million-in-education-funding/) $87 million in one-time school operations funding and over $10 million in school maintenance funding. In 2022, Dunleavy [vetoed](https://www.adn.com/politics/2022/06/28/dunleavy-signs-budget-that-will-send-alaskans-3200/) over $62 million for school maintenance.

Dunleavy’s spokesperson Jeff Turner declined to say on Tuesday whether Dunleavy would support a one-time or permanent increase to the education funding formula.

Majority lawmakers in the House and Senate have said since the beginning of the session that they would seek some form of an [increase to education spending](https://www.adn.com/politics/alaska-legislature/2026/02/10/majority-lawmakers-say-alaska-schools-need-more-money-from-state/) this year, arguing that last year’s formula change was insufficient.

But the kind of education funding increase proposed in the latest budget draft on Tuesday seemed out of reach when lawmakers convened earlier this year, facing down an austere revenue projection that made significant spending growth on state services unlikely.

ADVERTISEMENT

The war in Iran, which precipitated a sharp increase in the state’s projected oil earnings, changed that. The Department of Revenue [forecast](https://www.adn.com/politics/alaska-legislature/2026/03/13/dunleavy-administration-forecasts-hundreds-of-millions-in-new-revenue-this-year-due-to-higher-oil-prices/) earlier this month that the state will have more than $500 million in previously unforeseen oil receipts next fiscal year.

House majority lawmakers indicated on Tuesday that they would look to direct a significant portion of that income to public schools.

Rebecca Himschoot, a Sitka independent who co-chairs the Education Committee, said that dedicating $158 million to schools shows the House is “budgeting according to our priorities,” but that increasing the Base Student Allocation, rather than providing one-time funding, would be a more dependable investment in schools.

“Having the money in the BSA matters a whole lot, because that’s the Legislature committing to our schools now and in the future,” Himschoot said. “And one-time money, if that’s how it ends up — it helps. It just doesn’t help as much as the BSA.”

_\[_ [_Alaska Senate bill spurs debate over funding of homeschool programs_](https://www.adn.com/alaska-news/2026/03/19/alaska-senate-education-bill-raises-debate-over-correspondence-funding/ "https://www.adn.com/alaska-news/2026/03/19/alaska-senate-education-bill-raises-debate-over-correspondence-funding/") _\]_

In a hearing Tuesday morning, Republican minority lawmakers appeared skeptical of the proposed education funding increase.

“It’s jut an unwise thing to start doing big adds to your operating budget when you know they’re not sustainable multi-year,” said Rep. Will Stapp, a Fairbanks Republican. When lawmakers approve so-called one-time education funding, schools expect the same level of funding in subsequent years, Stapp added.

Stapp and other Republicans criticized the majority for allocating money to schools without finalizing the size of the Permanent Fund dividend. The new version of the operating budget draft was adopted in a 6-5 vote, with all minority committee members opposed.

“You prioritize what you value, so they are putting basically every other spending item in front of the Permanent Fund dividend,” said Stapp.

Majority members have said that they are holding off on finalizing the size of the Permanent Fund dividend until later in the budget-making process. Josephson said Tuesday that given the new oil projection, the dividend could be set around $1,300 per eligible recipient, above last year’s amount of $1,000 per recipient, even accounting for the education funding increase.

However, fellow Finance Committee co-chair Neal Foster, a Nome Democrat, said he “can’t vote for anything other than a full PFD.” Foster said the majority lawmakers on the Finance Committee are not in agreement as to the size of the dividend, which is why they have yet to set an amount in the budget bill.

Dunleavy’s budget proposal, which does not call for an increase to education spending, includes a statutory dividend at a cost of more than $2 billion to the state. Even if the updated revenue forecast comes to fruition, it would leave the state with a deficit of more than $1 billion next fiscal year.

Lawmakers have not followed the dividend statute in a decade, amid dwindling oil revenue that has increasingly made it impossible for the Legislature to sign off on a statutory dividend while balancing the budget.

Sen. Bert Stedman, a Sitka Republican who co-chairs the Senate Finance Committee, said in an interview Tuesday that he thinks the dividend will end up in the “range of $1,000.”

Senate majority members on Tuesday declined to commit to the education spending boost sought in the House. A bill introduced by the Senate Education Committee earlier this month would increase education spending by roughly $100 million, partially through a series of [policy changes](https://www.adn.com/alaska-news/2026/03/19/alaska-senate-education-bill-raises-debate-over-correspondence-funding/) that were greeted with skepticism during the bill’s initial hearing.

Stedman said that he was hoping to balance an increase in spending on school operations with an infusion of funding for school maintenance and construction.

ADVERTISEMENT

The state has been [spending less](https://www.adn.com/politics/alaska-legislature/2026/03/22/alaska-education-commissioner-says-school-maintenance-ranking-system-isnt-working/) than recommended on such projects since 2014, leading to a crescendo of complaints over [dilapidated buildings](https://www.adn.com/alaska-news/education/2025/03/08/a-rural-alaska-school-asked-the-state-to-fund-a-repair-nearly-two-decades-later-the-building-is-about-to-collapse/) with severe structural damage, particularly in rural Alaska. This year, school districts collectively requested over $800 million in state spending on maintenance and construction projects.

“At some point you gotta stop, take a look at your schools, and make sure your schools aren’t falling down,” said Stedman.

Stedman added that lawmakers should view the updated revenue forecast — which is predicated on oil prices remaining higher than they were before the Iran war started — with caution.

“We want to not get too euphoric over these current oil prices. We want to be a little careful as we go forward,” said Stedman.

I am against our municipal government appropriating revenues to our school district.

Five years ago, voters approved changing our school district governance to a directly elected, 9-member at-large body. This change eliminated the 5-member Board of School Estimate, with its 3-member council majority and 2 members from the mayoral-appointed BoE. The Township Council is not subject to any local body oversight. The Type 2 school district doesn’t eliminate any of the BoE’s preexisting authorities. They also are essentially the same powers as our council: setting policies, passing legislation, approving finances, and hiring & supervising “the CEO” that runs the organization.

Both governing bodies are directly accountable and must report out to the voters.

The Type 2 district brings the BoE the same taxing capabilities as the council’s. Specifically, the authority to petition voters via referendum to increase the tax levy (above the limits set by state law). Ballot questions can be for a one-time added levy or for a permanent, annually recurring increase — for operating needs or for capital financing.

The district leadership and its proxies are asking the municipal government for unrestricted contributions to the schools. The overarching justification is the council has a vested interest in the success of the school district. That the transcendent public good of educating Montclair’s children obligates any council to a policy of municipal assistance to the schools.

The advocates of financial assistance have identified the following funding sources:

- passing along savings from municipal efficiencies, workforce and constituent services reductions
- scaling back increases in municipal appropriations that do not provide at least the equivalent community-wide benefit as that of supporting
- the financial needs of our school district
- increasing municipal taxes and user fees
- creating inter-local agreements on a cost-plus, barter value, or no defined valuation basis
- expanding purchasing access to more favorably priced municipal contracts for good & services

Their purpose is to increase school spending. What they generally preclude is tax relief as a choice in applying these unencumbered revenues. Taxpayers will have less choice, less direct control over increased spending versus the alternative of choosing to tax ourselves more — by referendum. Further, non-tax revenues and surpluses are dynamic by definition and all behave differently over time. Our financial custodians’ tenures are also highly dynamic.

The schools levy is historically about 57% of our tax bills. The combined prior year and projected current year levies will reflect that 77% of the tax bite to our wallets goes to the school district. This excludes any added tax impact from Questions 1 & 2. As a separate governing body, the council has no control over school tax increases. Similarly, the council cannot restrict the uses of any revenues sent to the schools.

Frank Rubacky

Montclair

We now simply collect the taxes for the district and give them to them. That’s it. The New York City Council on Monday challenged Chancellor Kamar Samuels tofind savings in the Department of Education’s $38 billion proposed budget— the largest of all city agencies.

Mayor Mamdani in January ordered the school system, like the rest of local government, toappoint a “chief savings officer”tasked with making their department more efficient. Plans were due on Friday as agency heads face a tall order:Dig New York City out of a multibillion-dollar budget hole, with limited impacts to city services.

The education budget in a typical year is about a third of the city’s total financial plan, which has historically failed to account for actual spending. To right that wrong and still balance the budget, school officials said their submission included a “wide range of options,” such as adjusting noninstructional programs or cutting duplicative spending.

“Those are conversations that we are having now — not sure how much we had those conversations before,” Samuels said.

One of the areas where school officials hope to bring down costs is private special education spending by serving more students with disabilities inside the public school system. Those costs are reflected more accurately in Mamdani’s proposed budget plan than they were in years past.

“We’ve identified atremendous amount of fraud and abuse and simple misunderstandingthat this is not just, you know, free money,” said Liz Vladeck, general counsel for the public schools. “And so, we’ve taken, extensive steps to tighten up the process. We’ve made numerous criminal referrals.”

Council members pointed to areas of the education budget where they hoped to find savings.

“The DOE’s budget continues to have areas that appear to be overbudgeted. For example, the budget for books has been consistently overbudgeted when comparing actual spending to the adopted budget,” said Councilman Eric Dinowitz (D-Bronx), chairman of the Education Committee.

On average, the system has underspent $43 million on books each year, according to Dinowitz.

“We are definitely looking — I would say actually turning over all the couch cushions — to see where there’s underspend, especially now that we are under the executive order to achieve savings,” said Seritta Scott, chief financial officer of the public schools.

Council Speaker Julie Menin (D-Manhattan) pressed officials on the system’s whopping contracting budget, including agreements with outside consultants and technology firms.

There are roughly 3,000 active contracts with annual spending of $7 billion, according to Elisheba Lewi, chief procurement officer of the public schools. Of all awarded contracts, 6% are considered noncompetitive,commonly referred to as “no-bid.”

But the Council was split on a politically toxic issue of cutting school budgets, in response to enrollment declines.

Since the COVID-19 pandemic, mayors have largely funded schools at the same levels, recognizing the need for stability. But without federal aid that was provided during the public health crisis, city leaders have struggled with what to do now, with student enrollment projected to keep falling.

The enrollment declines, paired with the funding cushion, has also helped public schools lower class sizes in accordance with a new state law.

“We are seeing shifts in enrollments in our schools, andthere comes a time where we’re going to have to reflect that in our in our budgets,” said Councilman Lincoln Restler (D-Brooklyn). “Are conversations happening now around gradually shifting funding?”

“There are not many individual issues that we will discuss at any of these hearings that impact our collective vote on the entire $127 billion budget. That’s how important this is,” Restler added. “I really want to make sure we’re not in a situation where we’re seeing school budgets a day before the vote and … we need to vote ‘no’ on a budget because our schools are getting screwed.”

Councilman Phil Wong, a conservative Democrat from Queens, was more negative in his assessment: “At what point do we acknowledge, are we funding empty seats?”

Education officials said no final decision has been made on the funding policy for the upcoming school year.

“Nobody wants to think about removing funds, if you will, from a school,” Samuels said.

“So, we’re continuing to have those difficult conversations within DOE, and no decision has been made.”
